newsitem.title: USA: Hedge fund panel likes emerging mkt corporate debt.
newsitem.headline: Hedge fund panel likes emerging mkt corporate debt.

text.p: CHICAGO July 16 (Reuter), - Hedge funds looking to new trading opportunites should consider emerging market corporate debt, a panel of experts said Wednesday.
Panel members at the Managed Account Reports Conference on Alternative Investment Strategies also recommended increasing exposure to U.S. stocks.

Spreads for debt issued by corporations in below-investment-grade countries are "still quite wide compared to the U.S.," said David Reiss, managing director of Bankers Trust Corp.'s emerging markets portfolio.

He cited Russia, Bulgaria and other Eastern European countries as hot areas, as well as Hong Kong and South Africa. Latin American countries have lost their investment luster since spreads there have tightened relative to the U.S., Reiss said.

Most of the investments so far in emerging markets have been in sovereign debt, Reiss noted. But, with credit quality of countries on the rise, corporate debt has become a better investment -- and one that remains largely untouched.
"In the U.S. we are seeing a larger percentage of corporate and mortgage backed securities," Reiss said. "We see that as a huge growth area in emerging markets."
He predicted that in the next few years, the Brady bond market will shrink and corporate exposure will have to be added to emerging market indices like J.P. Morgan's.
Other worthwhile fixed-income investment opportunities include senior secured debt of U.S. banks, said Virginia Henneberry, managing director of ING Capital Advisors.
She noted that the secondary loan market has grown dramatically over the past few years as rating agencies have instituted formal programs to rate corporate loans,
Meanwhile, most U.S. bonds are not a good investment vehicle, said Mark Kurland, co-manager of New Castle Partners LLC and senior managing director of Bear Stearns Asset Management.
"I have no bonds; you can't make money with them," he said.
He criticized hedge fund managers who are "market neutral," rather than holding long positions.
"You can't make money being on the short side," Kurland said. "I am 100 percent long."
In that case, the only way he loses money is if the market goes down. But, he said, he would not lose much since much of the money is hedged.

Over the last 15 years the U.S. equity market has been up 15 percent, and 12 percent the last 50 years, he noted. He predicted the Dow Jones industrial average would reach 10,000 by the end of 1998 and 12,000 in 1999.
At at the same time, he said he agreed with economists forecasts calling for steady to lower inflation, as productivity gains increase.
Kurland said the best companies to invest in are large franchises and smaller spinoffs from big companies, and to have conviction in the stocks.
Still, it is "impossible" to pick which stocks will perform best, said Alphonse Fletcher, chairman of Fletcher Asset Management Inc.
Fletcher said that some of the best opportunites in the market are in digging up details that others don't know about.
"The best strategy is to buy 'em, hold 'em and that's it," he said. "Don't try to game the market because you will lose."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212 859-1867 ))
